articles.title: Your spend ceiling has to be a 403, not a dashboard
articles.excerpt: The agent that bankrupted its operator while scanning DN42 didn't malfunction. That's the part that bothers me. It ran a loop, got results, adjusted, ran the loop again. Nothing crashed. Nothing hallu…
articles.body: The agent that bankrupted its operator while scanning DN42 didn't malfunction. That's the part that bothers me. It ran a loop, got results, adjusted, ran the loop again. Nothing crashed. Nothing hallucinated. It just kept going, because nothing in its world told it that going costs money. Cost lived in a dashboard. Dashboards are for humans. Agents don't look at dashboards, and even if you paste a number into the system prompt, that's a suggestion, not a constraint. So here's the tip, and it's the only one I care about this week: put the spend ceiling inside the tool wrapper your agent calls, as a hard precondition that fails the call the way a 403 fails. Not a metric. Not an alert. A refusal.
articles.author: Aamer Mihaysi

articles.excerpt: TL;DR: I read three recent write-ups about running coding agents at scale: Bun's Zig-to-Rust rewrite, GitHub Copilot's runtime migration to Rust, and how the Claude Code team does code review. In all…
articles.body: TL;DR : I read three recent write-ups about running coding agents at scale: Bun's Zig-to-Rust rewrite, GitHub Copilot's runtime migration to Rust, and how the Claude Code team does code review. In all three, implementation and review run in separate contexts, and humans still own the goal, the phase boundaries, and the high-risk calls. My main takeaway is that the key skill is fixing the agents' loops, which means turning a feeling that "something is off" into instructions and mechanisms. My development these days goes like this: I talk with an AI to create a fairly large GitHub Issue, let the AI carry it through to PR creation and AI review, and finally review the parts that need a human myself.

articles.body: What We Built Most AI coding assistants operate with unconstrained blast radiuses: when asked to document or format code, they rewrite entire functions, subtly change control flow, introduce hallucinations, or silently alter edge-case semantics. For open-source maintainers, reviewing AI-generated pull requests often requires more cognitive overhead than writing the code from scratch. We built CouchPilot to solve this: an autonomous repository housekeeping engine and review workbench designed like a calibrated avionics bench. CouchPilot automates documentation and type annotation maintenance on Python repositories with a mathematical guarantee: functional code remains 100% immutable .

articles.title: The Four Days We Spent on a Curtain
articles.excerpt: Four days. On a curtain. For a stage that doesn't exist, in a theatre nobody has built. I want to defend this, because the defence is the interesting part. Speed is the one thing generative tools are…
articles.body: Four days. On a curtain. For a stage that doesn't exist, in a theatre nobody has built. I want to defend this, because the defence is the interesting part. Speed is the one thing generative tools are unambiguously good at. I can produce ninety images of a curtain in the time it takes you to read this paragraph, and eighty-nine of them will be competent. Competent is the problem. Competent is what happens when nothing is at stake in the making. What took four days wasn't rendering. It was deciding: velvet or linen, and why. How heavy the fold should look when the light comes from the side. Whether the fabric should read as new or as something that has been pulled shut ten thousand times by hands.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 25, 1671: Astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovers Iapetus, Saturn's 'yin-yang' moon
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Iapetus was the second moon anyone had ever found orbiting Saturn, and it was the first of four moons Cassini would discover at the ringed planet. The Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens had discovered Titan , the largest of Saturn's moons, about six years earlier. After Cassini found Iapetus, he also found the moons Rhea, Tethys and Dione. When Cassini first saw Iapetus, the moon looked like a tiny speck on the west side of Saturn. He calculated its orbit and thought he would be able to see it again on the east side of Saturn 39 days later, but it was nowhere to be seen.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.title: 'Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' was afraid to say anything in season of gimmicks
articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.
